$comment: Prefix rotation window (URL-CANONICALIZATION.md §3.3.8). A bumps its declared prefix from /v1/cluster to /v2/cluster. P's cached index.json still has the old prefix and continues to sign under /v1/cluster for up to one cert TTL (5 minutes). A's verifier MUST try the current prefix first; if signature verification fails, retry under the immediately-previous prefix. This vector pins the fallback-verify case.
name: prefix-rotation
scenario: A rotated prefix from /v1/cluster to /v2/cluster within the last 5 minutes; P still signs under /v1/cluster
$comment_verifier_steps: Step 1: A computes path-suffix under current_prefix /v2/cluster. A's a_received_url path is /mcp, which does NOT start with /v2/cluster — un-canonicalizable under current prefix. Step 2: A retries under previous_prefix /v1/cluster. Same problem (/mcp doesn't start with /v1/cluster either). The fallback case only succeeds when the path on A's side carries the OLD prefix; this vector pins the case where the proxy STRIPS the prefix end-to-end, so A's path-suffix derivation under either prefix yields /mcp (the empty-prefix branch §3.3.3 applies after the strip-fail). See §3.3.8 implementation note: when A receives a path-suffix-only request (no prefix at all), the rotation fallback applies vacuously — both current and previous prefix yield the same path-suffix. The non-trivial rotation case is when A receives /v1/cluster/mcp on the wire (proxy preserves the old prefix); A's current-prefix strip fails, previous-prefix strip succeeds, signature verifies.
$comment_receipts: Receipt commits to canonical_bytes_sha256_hex (the path-suffix /mcp). P and A reach the same hash regardless of which prefix A used in its strip step; the receipt's request_hash is byte-identical to what P computes. RECEIPTS.md §2.2.1 step 5 succeeds.
